lead: A line integral adds a field along a curve instead of across an interval. Chop the curve into tiny steps dr, dot each step with the field F at that point, and sum. For a force field this sum is work: only the part of the force along the road counts. Engineers use it for forces on a moving part, circulation around a wing section, and voltage around a circuit loop.
prereq: You need: definite integrals from Unit 2 and the gradient from 6.1; the potential shortcut is built in 6.3.

sections.h3: Adding a field along a curve

blocks.text: Let C be a curve in space and F = (F₁, F₂, F₃) a vector field. At a point on C, take the small displacement dr = (dx, dy, dz). The line integral of F along C is the sum of the component of F along each step:
∫_C F·dr = ∫_C (F₁ dx + F₂ dy + F₃ dz)
blocks.where: F₁, F₂, F₃ are the field components; dx, dy, dz are changes in x, y, z along C. The dot product F·dr uses only the part of F along the curve.

blocks.text: To compute it, parameterise C: r(t) = (x(t), y(t), z(t)), a ≤ t ≤ b. Then dr = r′(t) dt, so

blocks.where: r(t) is the position on C; r′(t) = (x′(t), y′(t), z′(t)); a and b are the parameter values at the start and end. Reversing the direction changes t from b to a and flips the sign.

items: Choose a parameter t and write x(t), y(t), z(t) for C.
Write the start and end values of t, in order of travel.
Compute r′(t) dt = (x′(t), y′(t), z′(t)) dt.
Substitute x(t), y(t), z(t) into F to get F(r(t)).
Dot F(r(t)) with r′(t), integrate from start t to end t.

blocks.text: Work done by a force F moving a particle along C is W = ∫_C F·dr. If F is in newtons and r in metres, W is in joules. A force at right angles to the motion does no work because F·dr = 0. A force opposite to dr gives negative work.

When C is closed, the line integral is written ∮_C F·dr and called the circulation. Circulation measures how much the field pushes around the loop. A fan blade, a wing section and a wire loop all have a natural circulation.

The value can depend on the path. In the worked example below, the same force gives 2/3 J along a parabola and 1 J along a straight line between the same two points. So work is not always just a difference of endpoints. 6.6 converts circulation round a closed plane curve into a double integral.

sections.h3: Path independence and the potential shortcut

blocks.text: Path independence means the integral from A to B is the same for every curve from A to B. For a plane field F = (M, N), a quick test is ∂N/∂x = ∂M/∂y. For a space field F = (F₁, F₂, F₃), the test is curl F = 0. If the test holds on a region with no holes, F is conservative and F = ∇φ for a scalar potential φ.

blocks.where: A is the start point, B is the end point, and φ is the potential. You do not integrate along C; you evaluate φ at two points. For a closed curve, the answer is zero.

blocks.text: If the test fails, the field is not conservative and the path matters. The worked example checks this: ∂N/∂x = −1 but ∂M/∂y = 1, so no potential exists and the two paths disagree. Find potentials as in 6.3.

figure.caption: Two routes from A to B, up through C and down through D, plus the straight chord. When the field is not conservative, the same force can give different work along these routes.

spec.aria: Two different routes from point A to point B plus a straight route, showing that the work done depends on which path is taken.

examples.question: A force F(x,y) = (x + y) i + (y − x) j acts on a particle. Find the work done from A(0,0) to B(1,1) along (a) the parabola y = x², (b) the straight line y = x. Then state whether the field is conservative. Take force in newtons and coordinates in metres.
steps: Take x = t, then y = t² on y = x². The start (0,0) is t = 0 and the end (1,1) is t = 1.
Then r(t) = (t, t²) and dr = r′(t) dt = (1, 2t) dt.
At r(t), F = (x + y, y − x) = (t + t², t² − t).
Dot product: F·dr = (t + t²)(1) + (t² − t)(2t) = t + t² + 2t³ − 2t² = t − t² + 2t³.
Straight line y = x: take x = t, y = t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Then F = (2t, 0) and dr = (1, 1) dt, so F·dr = 2t. W₂ = ∫₀¹ 2t dt = 1 J.
Test: M = x + y, N = y − x. ∂N/∂x = −1 and ∂M/∂y = 1. They differ, so F is not conservative; the two works legitimately differ.
examples.answer: The work is 2/3 J along y = x² and 1 J along y = x; the field is not conservative.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction
w1 = Fraction(1,2) - Fraction(1,3) + Fraction(1,2)
w2 = Fraction(1,1)
print(float(w1))
print(float(w2))

traps: Writing dx dy or dA where dr belongs. A line integral is along a curve, so it uses one parameter t, not an area element.
Reversing the direction of travel. Going from B to A changes the sign: ∫ from B to A = −∫ from A to B.
Assuming two paths give the same work without checking curl F = 0 or ∂N/∂x = ∂M/∂y. If the test fails, path matters.
Substituting y = x² into F but leaving dx and dy mixed. Replace both x and y and both dx and dy by their t-forms.
Ignoring the sign when force and motion oppose. F·dr negative means the field takes energy out along that step.

quiz.a: ∫_C F·dr = ∫_a^b F(r(t))·r′(t) dt; it adds the component of F along C.

quiz.q: Why does reversing the direction along C change the sign of a line integral?
quiz.a: Reversing C swaps a and b. The integral becomes ∫_b^a, which is the negative of ∫_a^b.

quiz.q: F = (3, 2). Find the work from (1,0) to (3,4) along the straight line joining them.
For F = (2xy, x² + 1), test path independence and find a potential.
quiz.a: M=2xy, N=x²+1; ∂N/∂x=2x=∂M/∂y, so independent. φ=x²y+y satisfies ∇φ=F; integral is φ(B)−φ(A).
Circulation is ∮_C F·dr around a closed curve.

quiz.q: Why can you not use φ(B)−φ(A) before checking curl F = 0?
quiz.a: φ(B)−φ(A) is valid only if F=∇φ. If curl F≠0 no such φ exists; using endpoints would give a wrong single answer for a path-dependent integral.

quiz.q: Evaluate ∫_C (y dx + x dy) from (0,0) to (2,3) along the straight line joining them.
quiz.a: r(t)=(2t,3t), 0≤t≤1; dr=(2,3)dt; y dx+x dy=12t dt; integral=6.

quiz.q: For F = (y, −x), find the circulation around the unit circle counterclockwise.
quiz.a: r=(cos t, sin t), 0≤t≤2π; dr=(−sin t, cos t)dt; F=(sin t,−cos t); F·dr=−sin²t−cos²t=−1; integral=−2π.

beyond: Not for the exam. Line integrals are how aircraft designers compute circulation and lift, how power engineers compute voltage around a loop, and how robot planners score a force field along a planned path. Search for 'line integral of a vector field', 'conservative force field', and 'circulation and vorticity'.
